column1: # Patches the tool catalog is allowed to call VERIFIED, and the real save that
# proves each one.
# verify-tools.mjs applies the patch's decrypt chain — exactly the codes the
# page's Decrypt button runs, via toolkit.js splitChain() — to the encrypted
# sample, and requires the result to equal the decrypted one byte for byte.
# A patch that is not listed here, or that fails, is not marked verified.
# Samples come from bucanero/save-decrypters (not vendored; pass its path).
# Paths are relative to that checkout.
# NO PATCH IN apollo-patches. These C tools have nothing to drive, so the page
# cannot list them however good the sample is: MC4 Cheat Decrypter, No Man's
# Sky, Terraria, PS2 APA Header Checksum. One more looks like a patch exists
# but does not: "Tomb Raider VI: Angel of Darkness Remaster" resolves only to
# Tomb Raider: Definitive Edition. A different game.
# MGS3 HD - Snake Eater was on that list and is not any more. BLUS30847 and
# BLES01419 each hold BOTH Metal Gear Solid 2 and Metal Gear Solid 3 as
# separate variants (see the 6th column below), and mgs-hd-decrypter's mgs2/
# and mgs3/ sample pairs prove one each.
# Uncharted: The Nathan Drake Collection (PS4/CUSA02826) has left that list.
# It is the naughtydog-decrypter's type-C format, the same one Drake's Fortune
# Remastered uses, so the patch is CUSA02320's byte for byte and the expansion
# pass proves it from there — no row of its own.
# Dead Island 2 (PS4/CUSA27043) stays out on two counts. Its title ID is not
# in psndb or apollo-saves, so nothing here can confirm it; and di2-unpacker is
# a chunked CONTAINER unpacker — start/end marker scan, reverse find, a loop
# over compressed chunks — which is the same class as Dying Light 2 and
# Revelations 2 Vita above. Those are deliberately unlisted: proving one means
# reading the payload back out of the engine's variable list, and that
# apollo-lib API is not being added.
# Call of Duty: Black Ops II on PS4 (CUSA57548) is a special case and is NOT
# written. The cipher would be a straight copy of the PS3 patch — 3DES-CBC
# with a hardcoded key over the whole file, byte-oriented, so endianness does
# not enter into it and cod-blackops-decrypter has a single code path for both
# consoles. What is missing is not the algorithm but the save: there is no PS4
# sample, only the PS3 GPAD0_CM.PRF pair that already proves BLES01031, and
# without one there is no way to confirm the PS4 profile's ':file' names. A
# PS4 Black Ops II save settles it.
# Resident Evil 3 Remake (PS4/CUSA14168) and Digimon World: Next Order
# (PS4/CUSA05392) WERE in that list. Patches now exist for both, verified
# against their samples. Title IDs came from the apollo-saves database (each
# title's README carries the official name), not from guesswork — a savepatch
# filed under a made-up ID would never match a real save and nothing would say
# so.
# Neither is active here yet, because the gate reads apollo-patches@MAIN and
# both patches are new:
#   CUSA14168 needs no row at all. Its code is byte-identical to Monster
#       Hunter Rise's (PS4/CUSA34119), so the expansion pass proves it the
#       moment it lands, the same way Resident Evil Village did.
#   CUSA05392, CUSA00053, CUSA04402, CUSA03856 and CUSA00057 each have a
#       checksum of their own, so each needs its parked row above. Un-comment
#       all five once the patches are on main.
#   CUSA00057 is the odd one there: the patch already EXISTS on main, it was
#       simply wrong, so its row must stay parked until the fix is pushed or
#       the gate goes red. Strider computes two CRC32 blocks — 0x04..0x77FF
#       written at 0x00, and 0x7804..EOF written at 0x7800 — and both ranges
#       and values were already right. Both were being written BYTE-REVERSED:
#       the save holds 76d63a5c / fbd43983 and the patch produced 5c3ad676 /
#       8339d4fb. Two missing `set [hash]:endian_swap` lines, the same pair
#       Far Cry 5, RE7 and Digimon all carry. With them the valid save comes
#       back untouched.
#       Fixed on the PS4 patches ONLY — CUSA00057 and CUSA00087. The sample is
#       a PS4 save (the C tool says so itself) and a PS3 save stores this
#       checksum the other way round, so the same edit on PS3/NPEB01297 and
#       PS3/NPUB31139 would be a guess dressed up as a fix. They keep their
#       original bodies, which also means they no longer share a chain with
#       the PS4 pair and stay unlisted until a PS3 Strider save turns up.
#   NPUB31564 (SAMURAI WARRIORS 4) looked like the same defect and was NOT.
#       Its patch is correct and untouched; the bug was in apollo-lib, and the
#       tell was that no verified PS3 checksum patch in the database uses
#       endian_swap — on PS3 the write is already big-endian, so needing one
#       would have made SW4 the odd one out.
#       `sw4_checksum` stores its four words as a 16-byte BSD_VAR_MD5 blob,
#       and the variable reader only converts host-to-big-endian for the
#       INT16/32/64 lengths — a 16-byte blob takes the default branch and is
#       passed through raw. So mid() sliced host-order bytes and the patch
#       wrote 6e0bc26c where the save holds 6cc20b6e. Correct on the PS3
#       itself, which is why it was never noticed; wrong on wasm and on PC.
#       Fixed in source/patches.c by putting the words in big-endian order
#       before storing them (BE32, a no-op on a big-endian host). The row is
#       parked until that reaches apollo-lib main.
#       The sample is a US save — sw4-checksum-fixer picks its region by
#       testing 0x58292, which is zero here while 0x58532 holds 13B2701A — so
#       the JP patches (PS3/BLJM61144, PS3/NPJB00534) are not exercised by it.
#       They need no edit either: the fix is in the engine, so they should
#       simply work, but nothing here proves it without a JP save.
#   CUSA14169 (Resident Evil Resistance) needs no row either — same Murmur3-32
#       code as Monster Hunter Rise, so expansion carries it, and CUSA14168
#       rides along with it.
# Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor (PS4/CUSA00053) and Shadow of War
# (PS4/CUSA04402) are written too, once their title IDs were supplied and
# confirmed against Sony's metadata. mearth-checksum-fixer dispatches on a
# "SAVE" magic to tell the two apart; a savepatch is per game, so each simply
# hardcodes its own layout. Mordor: length at 0x14, byte-sum from 0x18, stored
# little-endian at BOTH 0x04 and 0x10. War: length at 0x10, sum from 0x14,
# stored at 0x08.
# The double write is why Mordor was checked past the usual bar: "valid save
# unchanged" plus liveness would still pass if only ONE of its two offsets were
# being written, since both already hold the right value. Measured directly —
# poke a byte inside the summed region and both 0x04 and 0x10 move, agree with
# each other, and match an independent recompute.
# INTERACTIVE {TAG} CHOICES are supported (toolkit.js chainOptions, the 7th
# manifest column). A patch that references a `{TAG}a=One;b=Two{/TAG}` block
# from a required code gets a picker on the page, left deliberately unanswered
# — the engine starts at "nothing chosen" and so does the page, because
# defaulting would be a guess about which save the user is holding. Both L.A.
# Noire patches are listed below, four rows, one per console per branch.
# Two more patches in the database ask a question from a required code and
# still cannot be listed, for the ordinary reason: Sacred 2: Fallen Angel
# (BLJS10071, BLUS30312, BLES00410; {USERID}, eight profiles) and Devil May Cry
# 3 SE (PS2/SLUS21361; {SF}, ten save slots) have no reference decrypter in
# save-decrypters at all, so there is nothing to check them against.
# Not listed, deliberately:
#   PS4/CUSA07713  Monster Hunter World — decrypts correctly but exhausts the
#       MicroPython heap under wasm on its 8MB save (MemoryError, not
#       corruption). Revisit when the heap story improves.
#   PS3/BLES00485, PS3/BLUS30270  Resident Evil 5 (PS3) and
#   PS3/BLES01465 et al  Resident Evil 6 — both C tools ship a PS4-shaped
#       sample, not a PS3 one: re5-checksum-fixer's savedata.bin is the very
#       file that proves PS4/CUSA04437, and re6's has the byte-identical
#       16-byte header, with 0x00000008 at offset 0x8 where the PS3 patch
#       writes its DWADD. So the PS3 patches cannot be proved by it (measured:
#       "changed a valid save"). RE5 PS4 is already listed; RE6 has no PS4
#       patch in the database at all, so its sample proves nothing today.
#       Needs a PS3 DATA0.DAT sample for each.
#   PS3/BLES01880, PS3/BLUS31211, PS3/BLJM61093  Final Fantasy X / X-2 HD —
#       two REQUIRED codes that are alternatives, not a sequence: "Update
#       Checksums Final Fantasy X" (writes 0x64F4, range 0x40..0x64F7) and
#       "...Final Fantasy X-2" (writes 0x16268, range 0x40..0x1626B). Both
#       also write the shared header hash at 0x1A, so running the pair over an
#       X save leaves the X-2 hash there and the save is rejected — measured,
#       the harness reports "changed a valid save". Nothing here can pick for
#       the user: it is the SAVE that decides which applies. Needs the two to
#       become a {TAG} choice, or separate :file targets, upstream.
#   PS3/BLES01945, PS3/BLUS31270  Call of Duty: Ghosts — patch and C tool
#       cover DIFFERENT files. The savepatch fixes Adler32 over SAVEGAME.SVG
#       and is the only code in it; save-decrypters' cod-checksum-fixer (and
#       its sample) is MPDATA. So the sample cannot prove the patch. Needs a
#       SAVEGAME.SVG sample, not a manifest row.
# MULTI-TARGET is supported (toolkit.js chainTargets/routeChain): a patch whose
# required chain spans several ':file' targets gets one file slot per target,
# and each code is applied to the file its own target names. Dead Space 3,
# Prototype, Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 ReMIX and LUNAR Remastered are listed below
# and pass. Two rows in that class still cannot be listed, and neither wants
# the feature:
#   PS3/BLES01040 et al  Dead Space 2 — deadspace-checksum-fixer ships ONE
#       HED-DATA/USR-DATA pair and it is a Dead Space 3 save: BLES01733 passes
#       against it and BLES01040 does not. Needs its own pair.
#   PS4/CUSA01609, PS4/CUSA03199  Shantae and the Pirate's Curse — a container
#       patch, though nothing in it says so: its codes all target `:*` and
#       there is no `:~extracted\...` section. The giveaway is the engine, not
#       the patch — `decompress(offset, wbits)` stores what it extracts as a
#       BSD variable and never writes the file (patches.c ~2811), so
#       "Decompress Save" leaves the save byte-identical and only "Compress
#       Save" puts anything back. `Decompress(*, -15)` is correct as written:
#       `*` means scan the file for streams rather than take a fixed offset.
#       Its checksum half IS proven, in isolation: "Update JHash" over the
#       PACKED file (range 0x0004..EOF, +0x4900DC7C, written at 0x0000 —
#       exactly what shantae-pirates-curse-unpacker computes) leaves the
#       sample unchanged and reacts to a changed byte. Only the
#       compress/decompress pair is unverifiable, for the usual reason.
#       I had this filed under "sample and patch disagree" against
#       PS4/CUSA01587. That was simply the wrong game: CUSA01587 and CUSA02811
#       are Shantae: RISKY'S REVENGE, a plain fixed-range checksum
#       (0x027C..0x048F written to 0x0278) with no sample in this repository
#       at all. The unpacker's sample is Pirate's Curse.
#   PS4/CUSA12555  Dying Light 2, and PSV/PCSE00608, PSV/PCSF00728,
#       PSV/PCSG00594  Resident Evil: Revelations 2 (Vita) — CONTAINER
#       patches, deliberately left out. Their middle codes target
#       `~extracted\00000000.dat`, which apollo_apply_code reads and writes as
#       a BSD variable rather than a file, so what a run produces is a
#       recompressed container. That is not byte-comparable to the original —
#       zlib is not obliged to reproduce the input stream and measurably does
#       not (Revelations 2 Vita: 39,163 bytes in, 38,601 out; the reference C
#       tool unpacks both to the same payload). Proving one would mean reading
#       the payload back out of the engine's variable list, which is an
#       apollo-lib API this project is not adding. Both tools DO have sample
#       pairs (vita-re-rev2-unpacker, dl2-unpacker) if that ever changes.
# SAMPLE AND PATCH DISAGREE — the C tool and the savepatch are not looking at
# the same bytes. Not a harness limit and not a page limit; somebody has to
# work out which of the two is right. All measured as "changed a valid save":
#   PS3/BLES01894  Need For Speed: Rivals — the patch is fine; its SAMPLE is
#       not. USR-DATA is 716800 bytes but only the first 358404 were ever
#       encrypted, so no correct implementation can reproduce the .enc from
#       the .dec. Re-list it when the pair is regenerated from a real save.
# Waiting on a branch merge — the fixes exist, just not where the page reads
# from. The site fetches patches from apollo-patches@main at run time, so what
# matters here is main, not what is queued for the next console release:
#   PS3/NPUB30611, PS3/NPEB00686  MGS: Peace Walker — main still calls
#       `DECRYPT mgs_pw` with no save-type argument, so it decrypts nothing.
#       Fixed on branch mgs-pw-psp.
#   PS3/BLES00450, PS3/BLUS30248  NFS: Undercover — main still decrypts
#       `pointer+0x5B`, one block short of what apollo-lib has needed since
#       63f334a. Fixed on branch nfs-undercover-range.
# Re-add these four rows when those branches reach main; they pass against the
# branch content today (checked against each branch in a worktree).
# PS4/CUSA18008  Resident Evil Village needs NO row of its own. The patch had
# 11 cheat codes and no checksum code, so there was no step to run; it now
# carries the same "[Update Murmur3-32 checksum (Required)]" as RE7's
# CUSA03842 — which is exactly what save-decrypters' re7-checksum-fixer does
# for Village (murmur3_32 over len-4, seed 0xFFFFFFFF, into the trailing u32).
# Byte-identical code means the expansion pass below proves it from RE7 for
# free, the moment the patch reaches apollo-patches main. Listed here anyway
# because it was also checked directly against village-data001Slot.bin: valid
# save unchanged, and it reacts to a changed byte.
# The mgs-pw-psp branch also adds PSP Peace Walker patches — ULUS10509 and
# ULES01372 (mgs_pw(1)), NPJH50045 (mgs_pw(2)). They are correct, and this
# harness still cannot list them, because "equal to the reference plaintext"
# is the wrong test for them: libapollo deliberately leaves the 0x44-byte
# header word-swapped on PSP, so a savepatch reads the header fields the same
# way on PS3 and PSP. Measured against the shipped samples, the payload from
# 0x44 on is byte-identical and the header is exactly the word-swapped
# reference header — which is the documented convention, not a defect (see
# apollo-lib tests/test_samples.c, known_answer_mgspw_psp).
# Listing them needs a per-row comparison mode ("payload from offset N"), not
# a new sample. Worth doing when PSP coverage matters; not worth blocking the
# first release on.

# Five rows that used to sit here — Digimon World: Next Order, both
# Middle-earth games, Resident Evil 6 (PS4) and Strider — are live now that
# their patches are on apollo-patches main. They moved down to the
# checksum-only block with the rest of their kind.
# Samurai Warriors 4 is the one still parked, and not on a patch: NPUB31564 is
# correct as written and verifies UNMODIFIED against the sample. What it needs
# is apollo-lib's sw4_checksum host-endianness fix, which stored four native-
# endian words as a 16-byte blob the variable reader passes through raw, so a
# little-endian build wrote the checksum reversed. Fixed on apollo-lib branch
# `fixes`; pages.yml checks out apollo-lib with no `ref`, so the deployed wasm
# only gets it once that branch reaches main.
#PS3
# COMPARISON MODES, for the `expected plaintext` column.
# Default is byte equality with what the reference decrypter produces, and
# that is the bar. One opt-out exists, written per file:
#   prefix:PATH   the output must START with this plaintext. For the one case
#                 where the reference tool TRIMS the file and the engine does
#                 not — Metal Gear Solid HD's MASTER.BIN, where
#                 `DECRYPT mgs_base64` decodes over `range 0x0000,eof+1` and
#                 leaves the buffer 32 bytes long holding the right 21 bytes
#                 of payload. The payload must still match exactly and in
#                 full; only bytes PAST it are tolerated, the pass line says
#                 how many were ignored, and a run that comes back shorter
#                 than the payload fails. Harmless here because the pair
#                 round-trips: decrypt then re-encrypt restores both
#                 MASTER.BIN and DATA.BIN byte for byte (measured).
# It does NOT help the PSP Peace Walker rows further up. There the difference
# is at the START — libapollo deliberately leaves the 0x44-byte header
# word-swapped — so those still want a "payload from offset N" mode, which is
# a different relaxation and is not implemented.
# An optional 6th column picks a variant for patches holding several tools
# (Metal Gear Solid HD: 0 = Metal Gear Solid 2, 1 = Metal Gear Solid 3).
# An optional 7th column answers the patch's interactive {TAG} questions,
# `;`-separated, each `Value` or `TAG=Value`. The tag may be dropped when the
# chain asks exactly one question, which is every case here. Matching is on the
# value's NAME, so a patch that renames or reorders its choices fails the row
# rather than silently proving a different branch — and a row that leaves a
# question unanswered fails too, since the engine would refuse the apply.

# ---- checksum fixers ----
# These rows carry "-" as the expected file: the sample IS a valid save, and
# the patch has to leave it byte-for-byte alone. That is a real check — the
# sample holds the checksum the game itself wrote, so a wrong range, algorithm
# or write offset lands somewhere else — and the harness additionally pokes a
# byte and requires the checksum to move, so a code that quietly does nothing
# cannot pass by standing still.
# Each sample is attributed to the patch's own game: either the filename names
# the title ID, or the tool in save-decrypters covers exactly one game, or the
# filename echoes the game name. Samples that cannot be attributed are not
# used — several tools there cover a family of games that share one algorithm
# (the RE Engine ones, the Trails ones), and "a Resident Evil save proves the
# Monster Hunter Rise patch" is not a claim worth making. Patches left out
